lesson.title: Industrial Revolution Begins
lesson.summary: Why industrial production began in Britain, and how machines, steam power, and factories transformed textile manufacturing.
learningGoals: Explain how environmental factors contributed to industrialization from 1750 to 1900.
Explain how the factory system and new machines changed production.
lesson.bigIdea: Industrialization began in Britain because of coal and iron, agricultural change, capital, and overseas trade, and it transformed production through machines and factories.
lesson.context: Before 1750, goods were made by hand in homes and workshops, often in the putting-out system. Most energy came from muscles, water, wind, and wood.

sections.title: Why Britain

blocks.text: Britain had coal and iron ore near rivers and ports. Agricultural improvements and the enclosure of common lands raised food output and pushed rural laborers toward towns, creating a workforce for factories.
Merchants had capital from trade, including the Atlantic trade, and banks and a stable government protected investments. Colonies supplied raw cotton and markets for finished goods.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Cheap coal, available labor, capital, and colonial markets made machines profitable, so British entrepreneurs invested in mechanized production first.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: No single factor explains why industrialization began in Britain. Strong answers combine resources, labor, capital, and markets.

sections.takeaway: A combination of resources, labor, capital, and global trade made Britain the first industrial nation.

sections.title: Machines and factories

blocks.text: The spinning jenny and Richard Arkwright's water frame mechanized cotton spinning in the 1760s. Arkwright's mills brought workers under one roof on fixed hours, creating the factory system.
Steam engines freed factories from rivers. Mills moved into cities such as Manchester, near coal and workers, and production rose dramatically.

sections.takeaway: Mechanized textile mills were the first industry to adopt the factory system.

vocabulary.definition: The fencing of common lands into private farms in Britain, which raised output and pushed many rural laborers off the land.
A way of producing goods in which workers use machines in a central workplace on fixed schedules.
Richard Arkwright's water-powered spinning machine, patented in 1769, which helped launch the factory system.

connections.title: Atlantic trade and industry
connections.body: Profits and raw cotton from the Atlantic economy, including slave-grown cotton, fed British industry.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the Atlantic economy contribute to British industrialization?
connections.feedback: Name a specific link such as cotton or capital and explain it.
